123456.text: It topped SplashData's list every year from 2013 to 2019; in 2016 it alone was 4% of the passwords studied.
123456.evidence: SplashData table: rank 1 in 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019. "In the 2016 edition, the 25 most common passwords made up more than 10% of the surveyed passwords, with the most common password of 2016, "123456", making up 4%."

admin.text: Devices often ship with defaults like admin, and malware such as Mirai scours the internet for ones still using them.
admin.evidence: Manufacturers of such equipment typically use a simple password, such as admin or password on all equipment they ship, expecting users to change the password during configuration. ... active "worms" ran across the Internet searching for systems having the default username and password. ... In the real world, many forms of malware, such as Mirai, have used this vulnerability.

12345678.text: It's exactly eight characters, the typical minimum length; US NIST guidance now asks for at least 15.
12345678.evidence: Many policies require a minimum password length. Eight characters is typical but may not be appropriate. ... Passwords must be at least 15 characters in length (note that this was changed in revision 4 from 8 characters to 15 characters)

123456789.text: Research on PINs found that more than 35% of people who need a nine-digit PIN pick 123456789.
123456789.evidence: In fact, about half of all 9-digit PINs can be reduced to two dozen possibilities, largely because more than 35% of all people use the all too tempting 123456789.

12345.text: It's also a real ZIP code, used only by a General Electric plant in Schenectady, New York.
12345.evidence: The ZIP code exclusive to the General Electric plant in Schenectady, New York

password.text: MIT's CTSS was the first computer to ask for one, in 1961, switching off its printer so you could type it in private.
password.evidence: The Compatible Time-Sharing System (CTSS), an operating system introduced at MIT in 1961, was the first computer system to implement password login. CTSS had a LOGIN command that requested a user password. "After typing PASSWORD, the system turns off the printing mechanism, if possible, so that the user may type in his password with privacy."

Aa123456.text: It's built to pass mixed-case-plus-digit rules, which the US standards body NIST told sites to drop in 2017.
Aa123456.evidence: From 2004, the "NIST Special Publication 800-63. Appendix A," advised people to use irregular capitalization, special characters, and at least one numeral. ... However, in 2017 a major update changed this advice, particularly that forcing complexity and regular changes is now seen as bad practice: Verifiers shall not impose composition rules (e.g., not require mixtures of different character types ...)

1234567890.text: It's just the keyboard's number row, and row runs like this and qwerty can be tested automatically at high speed.
1234567890.evidence: The examples below illustrate various ways weak passwords might be constructed, all of which are based on simple patterns which result in extremely low entropy, allowing them to be tested automatically at high speeds: ... Common sequences from a keyboard row: qwerty, 123456, asdfgh, etc.

Pass@123.text: Swapping in symbols barely slows crackers: the admin password taken in the DigiNotar hack was reportedly Pr0d@dm1n.
Pass@123.evidence: Munged passwords (words with simple obfuscation): p@ssw0rd, l33th4x0r, g0ldf1sh, etc., can be tested automatically with little additional effort. For example, a domain administrator password compromised in the DigiNotar attack was reportedly Pr0d@dm1n.

admin123.text: Four of NordPass's top 20 are built on admin: admin, admin123, admintelecom and Admin@123.
admin123.evidence: NordPass 2025 top 20: 2 admin, 10 admin123, 18 admintelecom, 19 Admin@123.
